summary: Describes the detailed encapsulation to transport Frame Relay packets over an MPLS network as a pseudowire that supports Frame Relay services as faithfully as possible. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: Old Frame Relay data is packed into a modern network's packets so customers still get the service.

questions: what is a frame relay pseudowire
how does frame relay run over mpls
what is the frame relay control word
what is one-to-one mode in frame relay over mpls
subtitle: How a Frame Relay circuit is carried across an MPLS network as a pseudowire, using a 4-byte control word.

tldr.problem: Customers still had Frame Relay equipment, but their provider's core was an MPLS network. Frame Relay frames needed a way to cross that network and come out the other side intact.
tldr.mechanism: A pseudowire carries each Frame Relay virtual circuit. The ingress edge router strips the Frame Relay header and checksum, adds a 4-octet control word that keeps the congestion and discard bits, and pushes MPLS labels. The egress router rebuilds the frame.
tldr.outcome: The service is emulated as faithfully as practical, not perfectly. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 4619 is a Proposed Standard. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it remains the definition of this encapsulation.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 4619 describes a frame relay pseudowire: a mechanism between a provider's edge nodes that supports Frame Relay service over an MPLS packet switched network as faithfully as possible. Pseudowires (PWs) carry the protocol data units of layer 2 protocols across the network, and several can share one tunnel. They are set up with control protocols such as the one in RFC 4447.

A Provider Edge (PE) router must encapsulate Frame Relay information in a PW packet, send it to the peer PE, extract the Frame Relay information there, regenerate the native frame for the egress port, and do whatever else the service needs. Other layer 2 protocols are covered in separate documents, and the encapsulation is kept as common as possible across them.
sections.plainLanguage: A company's old Frame Relay lines are joined by a modern network in the middle. This document says how to wrap the old messages so they survive the trip and can be unwrapped at the other end.

sections.title: Applicability and Mapping Modes
sections.content:
The RFC says this service is not intended to emulate traditional Frame Relay perfectly. It lists the differences:

  • Frame ordering can be preserved with the OPTIONAL sequence field in the control word, but implementations are not required to support it.
  • The Frame Relay QoS model can be emulated, but that is outside the scope.
  • The BECN and FECN bits are transparent to the MPLS network and cannot reflect its status.
  • Switched virtual circuits and SPVCs are out of scope, as is the PVC link integrity check.
  • The Local Management Interface (LMI) is terminated locally in the PE connected to the Frame Relay circuit.

Two mappings are defined. In one-to-one mode, one Frame Relay virtual circuit maps to one pseudowire. In port mode, many virtual circuits on a port map to one pseudowire, and the encapsulation is identical to the HDLC pseudowire of RFC 4618. A port mode PW does not process Frame Relay status messages or alarms.
sections.plainLanguage: You can send each Frame Relay lane through its own pipe, or put the whole road into one big pipe. This is not a perfect copy of the old service, and the RFC admits that.

sections.title: Packet Format in One-to-One Mode
sections.content:
A PW packet is built from an MPLS transport header, a PW header, a control word and the Frame Relay payload. In one-to-one mode over MPLS, the transport header is one or more tunnel labels (four octets each), the PW header is a 4-octet PW label, then comes the 4-octet control word and the payload.

The tunnel labels let label switching routers carry the packet from one PE to the other. The PW label identifies the PW, meaning one LSP, assigned to one Frame Relay virtual circuit in one direction. Together they form an MPLS label stack as defined in RFC 3032.

The payload is the X.36/X.76 Frame Relay information field with bit or byte stuffing, the Frame Relay header and the FCS removed. Supporting a frame size of at least 1600 bytes is RECOMMENDED, and the two PEs MUST agree on the maximum payload length, for example through the MTU interface parameter at PW setup.
sections.plainLanguage: The Frame Relay message goes in an envelope with a small note on it, and that goes inside a bigger envelope with the address the network uses to deliver it.

sections.title: The Control Word
sections.content:
The control word is REQUIRED in one-to-one mode. It carries the Frame Relay information needed to rebuild the frame, plus an optional sequence number. Its layout, from the first bit:

  • Bits 0 to 3: MUST be 0, which marks PW data.
  • F (bit 4): the Frame Relay FECN bit. B (bit 5): BECN. D (bit 6): Discard Eligibility. C (bit 7): Command/Response.
  • FRG (bits 8 and 9): defined by RFC 4623.
  • Length (bits 10 to 15): used for padding removal.
  • Sequence Number (bits 16 to 31): a 16-bit unsigned circular space where 0 means the check is not used. Processing it is OPTIONAL.

If a link needs a minimum frame size (Ethernet is the example), the frame may be padded. When the layer 2 payload plus control word is under 64 octets, Length MUST be set to the PW payload length; otherwise it MUST be zero. The egress PE uses a non-zero value to strip the padding.

For backward compatibility, a legacy "martini mode" control word is also defined in which the B and F bits are swapped. It is used for PW type "Frame Relay DLCI (Martini Mode)".
sections.plainLanguage: The control word is a sticky note on the envelope. It says whether the road was crowded, whether the message can be dropped if things get busy, how long the message really is, and what number it is in the series.

sections.title: Encapsulation and Decapsulation
sections.content:
When a PE receives a frame on a Frame Relay UNI or NNI, it builds the control word from the frame. The C bit is copied unchanged. The DE, FECN and BECN bits are copied into D, F and B. A PE MAY additionally set D, F or B, for example as a result of policing or to reflect congestion it detects, but it MUST NOT clear a bit that arrived set to 1. The Length field follows the 64-octet rule, and the sequence number is handled per RFC 4385 if the PW uses sequencing.

On the way out, the receiving PE copies C/R, D, F and B back into the Frame Relay header (the F and B copies are MUST, and the PE may also raise FECN or BECN based on its own congestion state). It removes any padding, then does the standard HDLC steps: add the header, add any bit or byte stuffing, append the FCS, and queue the frame on the UNI or NNI.

For QoS, the Experimental Use bits of the PW label SHOULD carry the information, and higher labels in the stack SHOULD carry the same value. The ingress LSR MUST set the S bit of the PW label to 1, since it is at the bottom of the stack.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender copies the warning flags from the old message onto the sticky note and never rubs one out. The receiver copies them back, takes off any extra filler, and sends the message on.

sections.title: Control Plane and Interface Parameters
sections.content:
The PE MUST provide Frame Relay PVC status signaling to the Frame Relay network. If it detects a service-affecting condition for a DLCI, it MUST tell the remote PE the status of the matching PW, and the egress PE SHOULD generate the corresponding errors and alarms on the egress PVC.

Two bit orderings exist. The legacy one is used for PW type 0x0001, "Frame Relay DLCI (Martini Mode)", and the new one for type 0x0019, "Frame Relay DLCI". The type registry is in RFC 4446.

The PW setup protocol in RFC 4447 carries interface parameters that MUST be used to check that both ends can interoperate. This RFC adds the Frame Relay Header Length sub-TLV (0x08), an optional 16-bit value of 2, 3 or 4 octets, defaulting to 2 when absent.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the pipe works, both ends compare notes about what kind of old line they have. If one end sees trouble on its line, it tells the other end.

sections.title: Congestion Control
sections.content:
The MPLS network can lose packets under congestion, which affects the Frame Relay service. Because Frame Relay PWs carry many kinds of traffic, they may not behave in the TCP-friendly way described in RFC 2914. A PW that consumes more than its fair share while other traffic backs off SHOULD be halted.

Wherever possible, PWs should run over traffic-engineered networks with bandwidth allocation and admission control, such as IntServ with Guaranteed Service or DiffServ with EF. The RFC also notes that AF or DF may be used to lighten the load. If a virtual circuit's Committed Information Rate (CIR) is zero, "DF" would be appropriate. If the CIR is nonzero and DE is zero, "AF31" would be appropriate, and if the CIR is nonzero and DE is on, "AF32".

PEs SHOULD watch for congestion. On detecting significant congestion in received PW traffic, a PE SHOULD set BECN in frames sent on the same PW and FECN in frames sent out the attachment circuit. If the PW was set up with RFC 4447, its status notification can be used to stop the ingress PE from sending; the PW may be restarted manually or after a wait.
sections.plainLanguage: If the shared road gets jammed, the router puts up warning flags so both ends slow down. If someone refuses to slow down, their pipe may be shut off.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: PWE3 offers no means of protecting the contents or delivery of PW packets for the native service. It may, however, use security mechanisms from the MPLS tunnel layer. The RFC points to RFC 3985, RFC 4447 and RFC 3916 for a fuller discussion of PW security.
sections.plainLanguage: This pipe does not lock the envelopes itself. If you want them private, you rely on protection in the network around it.
